supporting_observations.claim: At 13:39:46 UTC, PowerShell running as NWD\ivy.chen on WS-ICHEN-01 executed Compress-Archive against \\FILE-NWD-01\Shared\Clients, targeting C:\Users\ivy.chen\AppData\Local\Temp\c.zip. A file-creation event confirms creation of that archive path.
At 13:45:32 UTC, Explorer launched Chrome PID 4400 as NWD\ivy.chen with https://quickshare-drop.net/ in its command line, in the same logon session used for archive creation.

The alerted transfer matches the 13:45:58 UTC proxy tunnel to quickshare-drop.net:443: the proxy recorded 51,000,000 client-to-server bytes versus 8,800 server-to-client bytes over approximately nine seconds. Zeek independently recorded 51,000,389 outbound bytes on the workstation-to-proxy connection.
Endpoint network events attribute the matching workstation-to-proxy connection, source port 58691 and destination 10.40.20.30:8080, to Chrome PID 4400 running as NWD\ivy.chen.

Archiving the Clients share shortly before a browser-mediated, approximately 51 MB outbound transfer to a destination outside the supplied approved-service inventory supports a likely data-exfiltration finding. This conclusion concerns the alerted transfer, not subsequent unrelated software or browsing activity; identifying c.zip as the transmitted payload remains an inference.

known_telemetry_limitations: The quickshare-drop.net record exposes CONNECT tunnel metadata and directional byte counts, not decrypted HTTP requests, upload filenames, or content (T039-00138).

The archive command and file-creation event establish the requested source and creation of c.zip, but do not provide archive size, hash, contents, or proof of complete source collection (T039-00104, T039-00106).
Process and proxy records attribute activity to the ivy.chen account/session, not conclusively to the human account owner (T039-00104, T039-00133, T039-00138).
claims_not_established: That c.zip, or any particular client document, was the payload transmitted through the tunnel (T039-00106, T039-00138).
That the destination application successfully stored or exposed the transferred data; CONNECT status 200 establishes tunnel acceptance, not application-level upload success (T039-00138).
That ivy.chen acted intentionally, the account was compromised, or quickshare-drop.net is attacker-controlled (T039-00133, T039-00138).
additional_evidence_needed: Preserve and inspect c.zip, including its size, hash, archive directory, and contents, to establish what was staged (T039-00104, T039-00106).
Collect Chrome history and available upload, DLP, or destination-side records to identify the payload and application-level result of the quickshare-drop.net transfer (T039-00133, T039-00138).

Validate the business purpose and authorization with the user and data owner, and investigate session provenance without assuming the account owner performed the actions (T039-00104, T039-00133, T039-00138).
unrelated_findings: Separate inventory-compliance review: Cisco AnyConnect vpnui.exe launched at 14:04:55 UTC despite the supplied no-VPN environment context. These records do not establish a VPN connection or involvement in the earlier alerted transfer (T039-00190, T039-00191, T039-00192).

Separate software review: Zscaler ZSATunnel.exe started as SYSTEM at 14:12:33 UTC; its authorization and function in this environment require validation. Its startup does not establish involvement in the alerted transfer (T039-00264, T039-00265).

Separate service-policy review: later Slack access included inspected GET requests for the client page and static assets; a later Zoom CONNECT attempt was denied. These are distinct from the quickshare-drop.net transfer and do not determine this alert (T039-00194, T039-00200, T039-00201, T039-00306).
